name: Apache Hudi
summary: A table format built for upserts and incremental pulls, with record-level indexes and built-in table services.
intro: Uber built Hudi in 2016 to apply database changes to its Hadoop data lake within minutes instead of rewriting whole partitions every night. Every record has a key. On each write, Hudi looks the incoming keys up in an index to find the file group that holds them, then either rewrites that file (copy-on-write) or appends the changes to a row-based log file next to it (merge-on-read). A later compaction folds the logs into new Parquet base files. A timeline in the table’s `.hoodie` folder records every commit, compaction and clean.

Incremental queries are the other half: a downstream job asks for “every record changed since commit X” and gets only those rows, so pipelines can chain table to table without rescanning. Table services for compaction, clustering and cleaning can run inline with writes or as separate jobs. Uber open-sourced Hudi in 2017 and gave it to the Apache Software Foundation in 2019; the current release is 1.2.1.
strengths: Efficient upserts and deletes by record key, which suits change-data capture from databases
Incremental queries turn any table into a change stream for the next job
Merge-on-read keeps write latency low for tables with heavy updates
Ingestion, compaction, clustering and cleaning services come built in
limits: More knobs than Iceberg or Delta Lake: table type, index type and compaction and cleaning policies all need choosing
Engine support is narrower: Trino’s connector is read-only and sees merge-on-read tables only as of the last compaction
Merge-on-read queries slow down when compaction falls behind
Writes are mostly Spark or Flink jobs

snippet.title: A merge-on-read table and an incremental read (Spark SQL)
source: order_id BIGINT, amount DOUBLE, updated_at BIGINT, order_date STRING
MERGE INTO orders t USING order_changes c ON t.order_id = c.order_id
WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET * WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT *;
-- only rows changed since a given commit

story: By 2016 Uber kept petabytes of data in Hadoop, and much of it changed constantly. HDFS files can’t be edited, so applying updates meant batch jobs that rewrote whole partitions every few hours, and late-arriving data forced rewrites of older partitions too. The usual alternative, a lambda architecture, ran a separate streaming layer next to the batch one, and its approximate results drifted from the batch numbers. Fast serving stores could take record-level updates, but they cost more to scale and usually kept only 30 to 90 days or a few terabytes of data.

Uber engineers including Vinoth Chandar and Prasanna Rajaperumal built Hudi in 2016 under the codename “Hoodie”. It applied changes to HDFS tables within minutes and let downstream jobs pull only the records that had changed. Uber described it publicly in March 2017, open-sourced it that year, and submitted it to the Apache Incubator in January 2019. By then it managed over 4,000 tables and several petabytes at Uber, and had cut warehouse data latency from several hours to under 30 minutes. Hudi graduated to a top-level Apache project in May 2020.
Recent releases have widened its scope: 1.0 in December 2024 added secondary indexes and non-blocking concurrency control, and 1.2 in June 2026 added vector search and Lance files for AI data.

choices.choice: Record keys and a pluggable index
choices.why: To update a record, Hudi must know which file holds it. An index (Bloom filters by default, HBase as an option) maps incoming keys to file groups, so only those files are touched.

choices.choice: Avro logs for writes, Parquet for reads
choices.why: Appending changes to row-based Avro log files is cheap; Parquet is fast to scan. Merge-on-read writes to the logs first and compacts them into Parquet later, trading some query cost for low write latency.
Recording each commit, clean and compaction with its time lets a reader pick file versions as of a commit and ask for only the records changed since one, which is what makes incremental pulls work.

choices.choice: Minutes, not seconds, on plain Hadoop
choices.why: Rather than add a fast serving store, Uber targeted workloads that could tolerate about 10 minutes of latency, keeping data in HDFS where storage is cheap and scans are fast.
